name: King’s Indian Defense
summary: The King’s Indian (…Nf6, …g6, …Bg7) hands White a big centre, then storms it with …e5 and a kingside pawn avalanche.
intro: The King’s Indian Defense, 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7, is the great counterattacking answer to 1.d4. Black allows a broad white centre and then detonates it with ...e5 or ...c5, often launching a full-blooded kingside pawn storm.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The King's Indian Defense is the archetypal hypermodern opening. Rather than contesting the center with pawns straight away, Black allows White to build a broad pawn front with d4 and c4, develops the kingside knight to f6, and fianchettoes the bishop to g7 where it eyes the long diagonal. The plan is to let White overextend and then undermine the center with a well-timed pawn break.

The two principal freeing breaks are ...e5 and ...c5. When Black plays ...e5 and White responds by locking the center with d5, the game acquires its most famous character: a race between opposite-wing attacks. In the more restrained lines Black may instead strike with ...c5 to open the position and exploit the active g7-bishop. Throughout, the tension between conceding space and generating dynamic counterplay defines the opening.

sections.heading: Pawn structure
paragraphs: The defining structure arises after ...e5 is met by d4-d5, closing the center. With the central pawns interlocked, each side has a clearly signposted plan on opposite flanks. White enjoys a space advantage and a natural pawn majority on the queenside; Black turns his attention to the kingside, where the closed center invites a pawn storm.

In the classic locked-center scenario Black plays ...f5, often followed by ...f4, ...g5, and ...g4, hurling the kingside pawns forward to pry open lines against the white king. White, meanwhile, advances with c5 and pushes on the queenside, using the b- and a-files and the minority or majority advance to create weaknesses and break through first. The mutual flank races make the King's Indian one of the sharpest and most double-edged of the classical defenses.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The King's Indian grew out of the hypermodern movement of the early twentieth century, which challenged the dogma that the center must be occupied by pawns. For a long time it was viewed with suspicion, but it gained full respectability in the mid-century as leading players demonstrated its rich attacking resources. It became a signature weapon of players renowned for their fighting style, notably Bobby Fischer and Garry Kasparov, who used it to play for a win with Black.

The opening remains popular at every level precisely because it offers Black an unbalanced struggle rather than symmetrical equality. Its reputation is that of a defense for those willing to accept some risk in exchange for genuine winning chances, and it continues to be a proving ground for dynamic, aggressive chess.

keyIdeas: Cede the center to White, then strike back with the ...e5 or ...c5 pawn break
The dark-squared bishop on g7 is Black's key piece, raking the long diagonal
A locked center after d4-d5 signals opposite-wing play: Black attacks the kingside, White the queenside
Black's thematic kingside storm runs ...f5-f4 followed by ...g5-g4 to open lines at the white king
White counters with c5 and a queenside pawn advance, aiming to break through first
The opening trades space and structure for dynamic, unbalanced counterplay

white: Establish a broad pawn center with d4, c4 and often e4, claiming space
Meet ...e5 with d5 to lock the center and gain a free hand on the queenside
Push c5 and advance the queenside pawns to open the b- and a-files against Black's position
Reroute pieces to blunt Black's kingside storm, for example a knight to d3 or e1 to guard key squares
Race to break through on the queenside before Black's kingside attack lands
black: Fianchetto the bishop to g7 and prepare a central break with ...e5 or ...c5
After the center locks, launch the kingside pawns with ...f5, ...f4, ...g5 and ...g4
Maneuver knights toward the kingside attack, often via ...Nf6-e8 or ...Nd7-f6-h5
Open the f-file or the h-file to bring rooks and queen against the white king
Keep the center closed so that White's queenside space cannot easily convert to a decisive attack first
